cards.summary: A monolith is one deployable application

prompt.text: A single deployable application that contains all of its features is a

answer.text: A single deployable application that contains all of its features is a monolith.

hints: From the Greek for one stone.
cards.fullLine: A single deployable application that contains all of its features is a monolith.

teaching.text: A monolith is not a failure. It has one deploy, one database and one codebase, which is often the cheapest way to find product-market fit.

teaching.alt: Close-up of a circuit board with many connected components on one board

cards.summary: A modular monolith keeps clear seams

options: Keeping everything in one giant file

hints: The seams matter, not the number of deploys.

teaching.text: A modular monolith organises features into modules with explicit interfaces. You keep one deployment while making a later split into services cheaper.

teaching.alt: A practical explanation of building a modular monolith and the lessons learned

cards.summary: A microservice deploys on its own

prompt.text: , so its team can ship without rebuilding the whole system.

answer.text: A microservice is independently deployable, so its team can ship without rebuilding the whole system.

hints: The key word is about releasing, not coding.
cards.fullLine: A microservice is independently deployable, so its team can ship without rebuilding the whole system.

teaching.text: The defining trait is independent deployment. Each service owns its data and talks to others over a network contract, which buys autonomy at the cost of coordination.

teaching.alt: A request moving through several small services that deploy independently

prompt.text: What is the main cost of microservices?

hints: More moving parts to deploy, observe and secure.

teaching.text: Every service adds deployment, networking, tracing and failure handling. A small team often spends more time on plumbing than on the product.

teaching.search: Monolithic vs Microservices Architecture Java Guides
teaching.alt: A comparison of monolithic and microservice architectures

prompt.text: In a layered architecture, each layer may call the layer
it, not the other way around.

answer.text: In a layered architecture, each layer may call the layer below it, not the other way around.

hints: Presentation sits on top of business logic.
cards.fullLine: In a layered architecture, each layer may call the layer below it, not the other way around.

teaching.text: Layers separate presentation, business rules and data access. The rule that dependencies point one way keeps the core from depending on the UI or the database.

prompt.text: What does an event-driven system use to connect producers and consumers?

teaching.text: A producer publishes an event such as order-placed. Consumers react without the producer knowing who they are. This decouples teams but makes the flow harder to trace.

prompt.text: Serverless removes the need to manage

answer.text: Serverless removes the need to manage servers while still charging per request.

hints: The cloud provider runs the code when an event arrives.
cards.fullLine: Serverless removes the need to manage servers while still charging per request.

teaching.text: Serverless platforms start code on demand and scale to zero. Cold starts, time limits and per-request pricing are the trade-offs to check against the workload.

prompt.text: CQRS separates the write model from the

answer.text: CQRS separates the write model from the read model.

cards.fullLine: CQRS separates the write model from the read model.

teaching.text: Command Query Responsibility Segregation lets each side use the shape it needs: a normalised write model and a denormalised read model. The cost is keeping the two in sync.

answer.text: The ordered history of events that changed the state.

options: The ordered history of events that changed the state
A copy of the user interface
correct: The ordered history of events that changed the state

hints: The log is the source of truth.

teaching.text: Event sourcing appends events instead of overwriting rows. Current state is rebuilt by replaying them. The history is valuable, but schema changes and replay cost real effort.

prompt.text: When should a team adopt microservices?

answer.text: When independent deployment is worth the operational cost.

options: When independent deployment is worth the operational cost
As soon as they have more than one developer
Whenever a conference talk recommends it
correct: When independent deployment is worth the operational cost

hints: Start simple, split when a real force pushes you.

teaching.text: Start with a modular monolith. Split out a service when a team needs to deploy independently, a part needs different scaling, or a boundary is stable enough to become a contract.
